newKeyTerms.definition: Actuality (act) is the way a thing really is right now; potentiality (potency) is a real capacity to be or do otherwise. To actualize a potential is to make it actual; change is exactly that. Things are “actual” or “potential” in these respects.
newKeyTerms.example: A cold cup of coffee is actually cool and potentially hot; heating it actualizes that potential.
newKeyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s *energeia* / *entelecheia* (act) and *dynamis* (potency); Latin *actus* and *potentia*. Defended in Feser’s chapter 1.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Mere logical possibility: a potency is a real capacity grounded in what a thing actually is (ice can melt), not just the absence of contradiction.

newKeyTerms.definition: The uncaused cause that terminates a regress of causes, above all a hierarchical series of things depending here and now on something else for their existence or activity. Also called the uncaused cause.
newKeyTerms.example: The purely actual actualizer of chapter 1, on which everything that changes depends at every moment.
newKeyTerms.origin: A standard term of classical natural theology (Latin *causa prima*).
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: The first event in time (e.g., the Big Bang): “first” here means first in the order of dependence, not earliest in time.

newKeyTerms.definition: A substance is a thing that exists in its own right (a stone, a dog); an accident or attribute is a feature that exists only in a substance and modifies it (its color, shape, size).
newKeyTerms.example: The stone is a substance; its gray color and round shape are accidents that exist only in the stone.
newKeyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s Categories; Latin *substantia* (“standing under”) and *accidens* (“what befalls”).
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: “Substance” in the chemical sense (a material like water or salt) and “accident” in the sense of a mishap.

newKeyTerms.definition: Saying something of something: the predicate is what is said (“is wise”), the subject is what it is said of (“Socrates”). Univocal, equivocal, and analogical are ways of predicating.
newKeyTerms.example: In “God is good,” “good” is predicated of God.
newKeyTerms.origin: Latin *praedicare*, “to proclaim”; Aristotelian logic.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: A property: a predicate is a linguistic or conceptual item; whether it corresponds to a distinct property in the thing is exactly what the simplicity debate is about.

newKeyTerms.definition: Made up of parts of any kind — physical pieces or metaphysical principles (matter and form, essence and existence, act and potency). Composition is the state of being composite; its opposite is simplicity (“noncomposite”).
newKeyTerms.example: A chair is composite in its pieces; a human is composite in body and soul, and in essence and existence.
newKeyTerms.origin: Latin *compositum*, “put together.” Central to the Neo-Platonic proof of chapter 2.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Complicated: a thing can be composite without being complicated (a two-piece object), and simplicity doesn’t mean poverty of perfection.

newKeyTerms.definition: A series in which each member causes only because it is being caused right now by the one before it, so the whole series depends at every moment on a first member that causes without being caused. A regress of such dependencies with no first member would be vicious — nothing would ever be explained.
newKeyTerms.example: A hand moves a stick that moves a stone: the stone moves only while the hand moves the stick (chapter 1).
newKeyTerms.origin: Scholastic *causae per se ordinatae*; contrasted with per accidens (linear) series like parents and grandchildren.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: A linear (per accidens) series extending back in time, like generations of ancestors, which the proofs do not need to deny could be infinite.

newKeyTerms.definition: Materialism: everything that exists is material. Naturalism: reality is exhausted by the natural world studied by science, with no God or immaterial realm. Materialists and naturalists deny that minds or causes are immaterial.
newKeyTerms.example: Paul Churchland’s argument that humans are purely material because they arise from purely material processes.
newKeyTerms.origin: Modern philosophical positions with roots in ancient atomism (Democritus, Epicurus).
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Science itself: naturalism is a philosophical thesis about what exists, not a scientific finding.

newKeyTerms.definition: The view that a human being includes an immaterial mind or soul, distinct from the body, not merely immaterial properties of a material brain. Dualists hold the intellect is not material.
newKeyTerms.example: Aquinas’ argument that since thinking is immaterial, the soul that thinks is immaterial and survives death.
newKeyTerms.origin: Plato, Descartes; Aquinas holds a distinctive hylomorphic version.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Property dualism, which denies an immaterial substance while positing immaterial properties of the brain.

newKeyTerms.definition: The physical law that in a closed system disorder (entropy) tends to increase, so order — and thus information content — tends to decrease.
newKeyTerms.example: A tidy room left alone becomes messier, not tidier; Davies uses the law to argue biological information must come from prior factors.
newKeyTerms.origin: Nineteenth-century physics (Clausius, Kelvin); cited by Feser via Paul Davies.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: A claim that order can never increase locally: it can, in open systems drawing on outside energy — which is why the environment matters in Davies’ point.

newKeyTerms.definition: Two opposite Pre-Socratic extremes. Parmenides denied that change (and hence potentiality) is real; Heraclitus, on a traditional reading, held that only change is real, with nothing stable (denying actuality). Feser argues both are incoherent.
newKeyTerms.example: The Heraclitean can’t coherently reason from premises to conclusion, since on his view there is no persisting self to do it.
newKeyTerms.origin: Parmenides of Elea and Heraclitus of Ephesus, 5th–6th centuries B.C.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Ordinary observations that things change or stay the same: these are claims that *only* permanence or *only* flux is real.

newKeyTerms.definition: Belief that there is only one God. Feser distinguishes monotheism in principle (there could not be another God) from monotheism as mere fact (there happens to be only one).
newKeyTerms.example: If God were one member of a genus, monotheism would be true only as a matter of fact, like Zeus alone on Olympus.
newKeyTerms.origin: Greek *monos* (“alone, one”) + *theos* (“god”).
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Henotheism (worshiping one god while allowing others exist): classical monotheism holds that a second God is impossible.

newKeyTerms.definition: God’s being all-powerful — the source of all power, with nothing outside the range of his power. Treated in detail in Part B (ch6b); in this module it appears as an example of a real attribute God has necessarily.
newKeyTerms.example: In Morris’s objection, omnipotence is the necessary property contrasted with the contingent property of having created.
newKeyTerms.origin: Latin *omni-* (“all”) + *potens* (“powerful”).
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Being able to do literally anything, including contradictions: the classical notion is power to do whatever is possible (see Part B).

newKeyTerms.definition: The ways something can be true or exist: necessarily, possibly, contingently, impossibly. Modal questions ask not just what is but what must or could be.
newKeyTerms.example: Asking whether God exists necessarily or only contingently is a modal question.
newKeyTerms.origin: Latin *modus*, “manner”; Aristotle’s modal logic.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Probability: modal claims concern what must or could be, not how likely something is.

newKeyTerms.definition: A number is an abstract object; a numeral is a symbol used to name it. Different numerals (“4,” “IV,” “four”) name the same number.
newKeyTerms.example: You can picture the numeral “2” on a chalkboard, but not the number two itself.
newKeyTerms.origin: Standard distinction in philosophy of mathematics (Frege).
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: The idea that erasing or imagining away numerals affects the numbers themselves — Feser’s reply to Schrader turns on this.

newKeyTerms.definition: Existing at all times, without beginning or end, but still within time and with a before and after. Everlasting things are “sempiternal.”
newKeyTerms.example: A God who had lived through every past moment and would live through every future one would be everlasting, not timeless.
newKeyTerms.origin: Latin *sempiternus*, “always-lasting.”
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Timeless eternity, in which there is no succession at all — the view Feser defends.

newKeyTerms.definition: Describing God in human terms as though he were a bigger or better version of us. Univocal predication tends toward anthropomorphism.
newKeyTerms.example: Picturing God as a very wise person who deliberates and changes his mind.
newKeyTerms.origin: Greek *anthropos* (“human”) + *morphe* (“form”).
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Analogical predication, which attributes perfections to God without importing human limitations.

newKeyTerms.definition: An argument that tries to prove God’s existence from the concept or definition of God alone (Anselm, Descartes). Feser’s proofs are not ontological arguments.
newKeyTerms.example: Reasoning that since God is the greatest conceivable being, he must exist in reality.
newKeyTerms.origin: Anselm’s Proslogion (11th century); named by Kant.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Feser’s claim that God exists necessarily, which is derived from what the proofs show about the world’s cause, not from a definition.

newKeyTerms.definition: The charge, pressed by some contemporary critics, that if God is simple and his act of creating is identical with his necessary essence, then everything God does — and the world itself — would be necessary.
newKeyTerms.example: “If creating is identical to God, and God is necessary, then creating is necessary.”
newKeyTerms.origin: Contemporary philosophy of religion (e.g., R. T. Mullins); not raised in this chapter.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Morris’s objection: Morris argues that necessary and contingent properties can’t be identical; modal collapse argues simplicity forces everything to be necessary. Both are addressed with the real/Cambridge distinction.

newKeyTerms.definition: The most basic entities in current physics, not composed of other particles. Fermions make up matter (like electrons and quarks); bosons carry forces (like photons).
newKeyTerms.example: Feser notes that even an electron has distinct attributes (mass, charge, spin) and can come into being and pass away — so it involves composition and potency.
newKeyTerms.origin: Named after physicists Enrico Fermi and Satyendra Nath Bose.
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Simple beings in Feser’s sense: not being made of smaller particles is not the same as having no parts or potentialities at all.

newKeyTerms.definition: Giving to something created the worship due only to God. Feser says worshiping a non-simple “god” would be idolatry, since such a being would be a creature.
newKeyTerms.example: Worshiping a powerful superangel as if it were the ultimate source of all being.
newKeyTerms.origin: Greek *eidolon* (“image”) + *latreia* (“worship”).
newKeyTerms.confuseWith: Merely having an inadequate concept of God: idolatry concerns what is worshiped, not how precisely it is understood.

definitionNotes.Equivocal predication: Adverb: used “equivocally”; the ambiguity is called “equivocation.”
definitionNotes.Analogical predication: Adverb: used “analogically”; the things so related are “analogates.”
definitionNotes.Substantial form and prime matter: The theory that material things are form-matter composites is called “hylomorphism” (adjective “hylomorphic”).
definitionNotes.Genus and specific difference: The specific difference is also called the “differentia.”
